turns.doctor_question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Um, so, what brings me in... well, it's been a long time coming, I guess. I've always been a bit on the go, but what finally pushed me to actually make the appointment and come in today is this... this thing I keep doing, especially at work, but really in my personal life too. 

I'm a software developer, right? So we have these long sprint planning meetings, which are incredibly important for figuring out our workload for the next couple of weeks. And I just... I keep getting up. Like, physically leaving my seat right in the middle of it. And it's not just work, it happened just the other day when I was on a really important call with my mortgage broker. I know, logically, I should just stay put. I know it's important and I need to be listening and present. But I get this sudden urge, and I'll just stand up because I'll convince myself I absolutely need a glass of water right that very second, or I'll suddenly remember something in the other room and I just decide to go check it right then and there. 

And then I'm walking back to my desk and I'm thinking, 'Why did I just do that? I'm forty years old, I can sit through a professional meeting or a financial call.' But it's like my brain just decides we're moving now, and I can't seem to just stay in my chair when I'm supposed to. It’s just getting so frustrating to constantly be fighting this urge to walk away from things I really need to be focusing on.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly describes frequently leaving their seat during important work meetings and calls when they are expected to remain seated.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have similar trouble staying seated when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow, yes. Yes, absolutely. I mean, it’s actually kind of funny you ask that, because when I look back, it’s like a completely unbroken line from then to now. I grew up in this really small town, and the elementary school was so tiny that everyone knew everyone, and all the teachers talked to each other, right? So my reputation definitely preceded me. 

I distinctly remember in third grade—Mrs. Gable’s class—she actually had to move my desk right up next to hers. Not because I was a bad kid or anything, but because I just... I was always popping up out of my seat. Always. Like a jack-in-the-box. We’d be right in the middle of a spelling lesson, and I’d just be up, wandering over to the pencil sharpener, or going to look out the window because I thought I saw a bird, or just standing up beside my desk for absolutely no reason. 

And it wasn’t just the standing, either. I was constantly getting reminded to stay in my seat, but I was also the kid who would just blurt out the answer before she even finished asking the question. Like, my hand would go up, but the words were already out of my mouth before she could even say my name. And the schoolwork itself... I was smart, I understood the material, but I would just rush through it so incredibly fast. I’d finish a worksheet in two minutes flat, hand it in with all these careless mistakes, and then just be sitting there vibrating because I had nothing to do and I couldn’t stand just sitting there waiting for everyone else to finish. So, yeah, the teachers were constantly having to manage me, moving my desk, reminding me to sit down, telling me to slow down... it was definitely a whole thing back then, too.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes rushing through schoolwork and handing it in with 'careless mistakes'.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as looking out the window because they thought they saw a bird.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly confirms frequently leaving their seat in class, describing themselves as 'always popping up out of my seat'.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling restless, noting they would be 'sitting there vibrating' when forced to wait.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient states they would 'blurt out the answer before she even finished asking the question'.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often have trouble sustaining attention on tasks, even when you’re trying to focus?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes and no. I mean, it's not like I can't focus on *anything*, but when it comes to the things I'm actually supposed to be doing, the things I *need* to do... yeah, it's a real struggle. And it's so frustrating because I really, truly want to focus. I'll sit down, right? I'll get my coffee, I'll close all my extra browser tabs, I'll put my phone on silent. I'll do all the things you're supposed to do to be productive. 

Take work, for example. As a developer, a big part of my job is reviewing other people's code—pull requests, we call them. It's detailed work, you have to really understand what they're trying to do and spot any potential issues. And I'll open one up, and I'll have the best intentions. I'll be like, "Okay, I'm going to knock this out right now." But then, I don't know, maybe three or four minutes go by, and I'll suddenly realize I've been staring at the exact same block of code the entire time, but I haven't actually processed a single line of it. Because in my head, I'm thinking about what I'm going to make for dinner, and then that makes me think about how I need to go to the grocery store, and then I remember that I need to pick up dry cleaning, and oh, I wonder if that new sci-fi movie is streaming yet, and did I ever reply to my sister's text from yesterday? It's just this cascade of thoughts.

And it happens with personal stuff, too. Like those mortgage documents I mentioned earlier. I really needed to read through them carefully—it's a huge financial commitment, obviously. But I'd sit there, trying to read the fine print, and my eyes would just be scanning the words while my brain was a million miles away, thinking about five completely unrelated things all at once. I have to physically force myself to go back and re-read the same paragraph three or four times just to make it stick. So, yes, I guess sustaining that attention, actually keeping it locked onto the task at hand when my brain wants to be anywhere else... that's definitely a big part of the problem.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly confirms struggling to sustain attention on tasks like reviewing code or reading mortgage documents, often having to re-read paragraphs multiple times.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by a cascade of unrelated thoughts while trying to focus on tasks.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a period where your mood was unusually high, euphoric, or irritable for days at a time?
turns.patient_response:
No, I don't think so. I mean, not like what you're describing, where it's just this constant high or irritability for days on end. I definitely get frustrated, like I was saying before with the code reviews and having to re-read everything a million times. That makes me irritable, for sure, but it's very situational, you know? It's directly tied to whatever I'm struggling with in that exact moment. It's not this overarching mood that just settles over me for days at a time. 

And as for being euphoric or unusually high... no, definitely not. I'll get excited about things, of course. Like if I finally figure out a bug in the code that's been driving everyone crazy for a week, I'll be thrilled. I might even do a little victory dance at my desk. But that's just normal happiness, right? It's not like I feel invincible or like I don't need sleep or anything extreme like that. My moods are pretty much just normal reactions to whatever is happening in my life at the time, even if I do get a bit more wound up or frustrated than maybe some other people do when I can't just sit still and get my work done. But yeah, no periods of days at a time like you're asking about. It's just the constant sort of... buzzing energy that I've always had.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes having a 'constant sort of... buzzing energy' that they have always had, indicating being 'on the go' or driven by a motor.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly denies experiencing periods of unusually high, euphoric, or irritable moods lasting for days at a time.
symptom_reasoning.S035: The patient denies feeling 'invincible', indicating an absence of inflated self-esteem or grandiosity.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly denies feeling like they do not need sleep.

turns.doctor_question: Do you have recurrent intrusive thoughts or urges that feel hard to dismiss and push you to do certain behaviors over and over?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I have thoughts that bounce around constantly, like I was saying with the grocery store and the dry cleaning and the movie, but they aren't... they aren't *intrusive* in the way you're describing, where they feel like they're forcing me to do something over and over again. 

I mean, sure, I might tap my foot, or I have this habit of clicking my pen—my coworkers used to joke about it before we all went remote, I'd just sit there clicking the top of my pen during meetings—click, click, click—but that's not because I have some overwhelming urge or thought telling me I *have* to do it. It's just... it's just excess energy, you know? It's like a release valve. If I'm sitting in a long meeting, especially one that could have been an email, my body just needs to be doing *something*. So the pen clicking, or shifting in my chair, or getting up to grab my third glass of water... it's just me trying to physically cope with having to sit still. 

It's not like I'm thinking, "Oh, I have to click this pen ten times or something bad will happen." There's no ritual to it, no specific thought driving it. It's almost unconscious half the time. My husband will actually reach over and gently put his hand on my knee when we're watching TV because I'll be bouncing my leg so hard the whole couch is shaking, and I won't even realize I'm doing it until he points it out. So, no, no thoughts pushing me to do things repeatedly. Just a lot of physical restlessness that kind of spills out on its own.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions getting up to grab water during long meetings as a way to cope with having to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly notes having 'excess energy' and 'a lot of physical restlessness'.
symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient explicitly denies having intrusive thoughts that force them to do things repeatedly.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient clarifies that their repetitive physical behaviors are not driven by overwhelming urges, rituals, or thoughts that something bad will happen.
